segments.en: The kettle clicks off, someone asks, fancy a cuppa, and before you know it there's a mug of tea in your hands. In the United Kingdom, a good chat often starts exactly like this.
The UK is made up of four nations sharing one set of islands: England, Scotland, Wales and Northern Ireland. Each has its own character, its own accents and its own proud traditions.

London, the capital, stretches along the River Thames. Red double-decker buses roll past the Houses of Parliament, the bell called Big Ben chimes the hours, and the Tower of London has guarded the river for nearly a thousand years.

Head north into Scotland and the land rises into misty Highlands and deep lochs. In Edinburgh, a castle perches on an old volcanic rock, and you may hear the skirl of bagpipes drifting down the Royal Mile.
In Wales, green valleys meet rugged mountains and a coastline of cliffs and castles. Welsh is spoken alongside English, and road signs appear in both. Croeso, they say, which means welcome.
Northern Ireland has the Giant's Causeway, thousands of six-sided stone columns stepping into the sea, formed by ancient lava but wrapped in legends about a giant named Finn McCool.
British people are known for politeness. Queueing patiently is taken seriously, and you will hear please, thank you and sorry many times a day, sometimes even when nothing has gone wrong.
The weather changes quickly, so it is a favourite topic of conversation. A sunny morning can turn to drizzle by lunchtime, which is why an umbrella is never far away.

Food ranges from fish and chips wrapped in paper at the seaside to a Sunday roast with gravy and Yorkshire puddings. Afternoon tea brings scones with jam and clotted cream, and in cities you will find flavours from all over the world.
Many sports were first organised here, including football, rugby, cricket and tennis. On a Saturday afternoon, football stadiums roar with songs and chants.

This is also a land of stories. Shakespeare wrote his plays here, and so did the authors behind Peter Rabbit, Alice in Wonderland and a certain young wizard. Music too, from the Beatles to today's pop stars.
In the countryside, footpaths wind between hedgerows and stone walls, past thatched cottages and village pubs, where walkers stop for a warm meal by the fire.
So pop the kettle on one last time, then cross the Irish Sea to the west, where Ireland is waiting with a céad míle fáilte, a hundred thousand welcomes.
